biographics.title: Owner of a growing service business (hotel group, clinic network, real estate agency, recruiting firm, or e-commerce brand) with 15-150 staff
biographics.status: Married, kids, business is the family's main asset
biographics.location: US, UK, UAE, or EU. Mid-size city. Hands-on in the business every day.
biographics.education: Business degree or came up through the industry. Not technical, and doesn't want to be.
biographics.personal_income: $150k-$400k depending on the year; the business does $2M-$20M in revenue

psychographics.values: Reliability and straight talk. Wants one accountable person, not an account manager relaying messages to juniors. Judges people by whether they do what they said, when they said.
psychographics.belief_system: The business grew faster than its systems. Spreadsheets, WhatsApp, a dated website, and five tools that don't talk to each other got us here, but they're now the thing slowing us down.
psychographics.fears: Hiring the wrong developer again. He's been burned before: a cheap freelancer who disappeared, or an agency that sent juniors and shipped late. He can't evaluate technical work himself, so trust is everything.
psychographics.spending_logic: Will invest $20k-$50k, often phased, to remove friction his staff and customers complain about every week. He doesn't need an ROI spreadsheet; he needs to believe the person will actually deliver and stick around after launch.

the_crap_he_deals_with: His front desk retypes the same booking into three systems. Customers call because the website form doesn't work on phones, or they give up mid-booking and go to a competitor with a smoother flow. His best admin threatens to quit every busy season because the manual workload doubles. Reports are assembled by hand in Excel every Monday. He knows technology should fix this, but every past attempt either stalled or made things more complicated.
the_hunger: One trusted senior partner who understands the business first, then quietly replaces the friction: a booking flow that works, systems that talk to each other, automation for the repetitive work, and a website that doesn't embarrass him. Someone who explains things in plain language, sends updates without being chased, and is still reachable six months after launch.

trifecta_alignment.joy: End-to-end ownership of a real business system: booking and intake flows, integrations between tools, dashboards the owner actually reads, automation and AI assistants for the repetitive work.
trifecta_alignment.money: A $20k-$50k phased engagement the owner approves directly, with a first phase small enough to prove the partnership and a roadmap that extends it naturally.
trifecta_alignment.mission: Removing friction so the staff stop fighting their tools and customers stop feeling it. Every digital interaction with the business should build trust, not test patience.

cost_of_inaction: Every week the friction stays: staff hours lost to double entry and manual reports, customers who abandon a clunky booking and don't call to complain (they just book elsewhere), slow replies that make the business look smaller than it is, and the best employees quietly burning out on work a system should do. The busy season magnifies all of it.
trigger_events: A key admin or office manager resigned, citing the manual workload, and the owner realized the process lives in that person's head.
A competitor launched online booking or a customer portal, and customers started mentioning it.
The busy season overwhelmed the current setup: double bookings, missed enquiries, or a weekend of angry calls.
A previous freelancer or agency engagement failed, and the half-finished system is now part of the problem.
The owner tried an off-the-shelf tool and hit its limits within months; the workarounds are now their own workload.
hiring_threshold: 1. FRICTION IS FELT DAILY: the owner, staff, or customers can name the specific annoyance without thinking (the retyping, the broken form, the Monday report). 2. TRUST IS ESTABLISHED: he has seen proof of reliability: real projects, testimonials that mention communication and delivery, direct access to the senior person doing the work. 3. THE FIRST STEP IS SMALL: a scoped first phase he can approve without betting the year's budget.

biographics.title: Non-technical founder or co-founder of a digital product or productized service ($200k-$3M revenue, 2-20 people)
biographics.status: Single or young family; the product is her main bet
biographics.education: Domain expert: came from the industry her product serves (health, recruiting, hospitality, professional services). Not a developer.
biographics.personal_income: $80k-$200k; funding is revenue, savings, or a small angel round

psychographics.values: Momentum and honesty. She would rather hear 'that feature is a bad idea, here's a simpler way' than watch a polite contractor build the wrong thing for three months.
psychographics.belief_system: The product idea is validated; execution is the bottleneck. What kills companies like hers isn't competition, it's shipping slowly and building on foundations that fall over at the worst moment.
psychographics.fears: Being technically hostage: to an agency that hands her project between juniors, to a codebase nobody can maintain, or to a developer she can't evaluate. She's seen founder friends lose a year and their runway this way.
psychographics.spending_logic: Will invest $20k-$60k to build or rebuild the product properly with a senior partner who works directly with her. She's comparing this against agency quotes twice the price with half the accountability.

the_crap_he_deals_with: Her MVP was built by a contractor who's gone. Small changes take weeks and break other things. Customers ask for features she can't promise because she doesn't know what the codebase can take. Ops behind the product are held together with spreadsheets and manual steps that eat her evenings. Agencies she's talked to pitch big teams and bigger retainers, but she can never talk to the person actually writing the code.
the_hunger: A senior technical partner who acts like a co-founder for the build: tells her what to build and what to skip, ships a product customers enjoy using, automates the manual ops behind it, and leaves her with a system her next hire can take over. Direct communication, visible progress every week, no handoffs.

trifecta_alignment.joy: Product engineering with real ownership: MVP builds and rebuilds, AI features that serve the product instead of decorating it, automation of the founder's manual ops, clean handover.
trifecta_alignment.money: A $20k-$60k build or rebuild, often followed by a monthly partnership for iteration, approved by the founder herself in days, not quarters.
trifecta_alignment.mission: Giving a domain expert a product and operation that match the quality of her idea, so execution stops being the bottleneck.

cost_of_inaction: Every month of slow shipping is a month of runway spent standing still: features customers asked for stay unbuilt, the manual ops behind the product eat the founder's evenings, and every small change that breaks something teaches customers not to trust the product. Competitors with faster execution set the pace she gets measured against.
trigger_events: Her contractor or dev shop disappeared, went unresponsive, or delivered something she can't extend.
A wave of customer feedback demands product changes she can't ship with the current setup.
She raised a small round or landed a big client, and the product now has to hold up under real usage.
An agency quote came in at 2-3x her budget with a team she'd never talk to directly.
Her own evenings became the ops department: manual onboarding, manual reports, manual support.
hiring_threshold: 1. FRICTION IS FELT DAILY: shipping is visibly slow, ops are visibly manual, and she can name what she'd build next if she trusted the foundation. 2. TRUST IS ESTABLISHED: she's seen real shipped products, testimonials that mention honesty and communication, and she talks directly to the senior person from the first call. 3. THE FIRST STEP IS SMALL: an audit or scoped first milestone that proves the working style before the bigger build.

biographics.title: Operations or general manager at a growing business (30-200 staff), reporting to an owner who signs off on spending
biographics.status: The person everyone messages when a system breaks
biographics.education: Rose through operations; expert in how the business actually runs, fluent in its spreadsheets
biographics.personal_income: $70k-$140k; spends the owner's money carefully because failures land on her

psychographics.values: Practicality. She doesn't want innovation theater; she wants the Monday report to build itself and the intake queue to stop leaking.
psychographics.belief_system: The team isn't slow, the tools are. People are copy-pasting between systems that were never connected, and every workaround becomes permanent.
psychographics.fears: Championing a technology project that fails publicly. If she brings in a developer and it goes badly, it's her credibility with the owner that pays for it.
psychographics.spending_logic: Builds the case for a $20k-$50k engagement by listing what the team could stop doing manually. Needs a partner who makes her look right: clear scope, visible progress, no surprises.

the_crap_he_deals_with: Her team runs the business across five tools plus email, and she personally maintains the spreadsheets that bridge them. New staff take weeks to learn the workarounds. Customer-facing steps (quotes, scheduling, follow-ups) depend on someone remembering. She's evaluated off-the-shelf tools; each fixes a third of the problem and adds its own quirks. She needs custom glue and automation, but past developer experiences were slow and opaque.
the_hunger: A senior partner who maps how work actually flows, then connects the systems, automates the handoffs, and gives her team one place to look. Someone who communicates in her language, shows progress weekly, and trains the team instead of leaving a mystery box.

trifecta_alignment.joy: Workflow automation and integrations: connecting the CRM to the scheduling tool, automating intake and follow-ups, AI assistants for the repetitive queue, dashboards that replace the Monday spreadsheet ritual.
trifecta_alignment.money: A $20k-$50k engagement she champions and the owner approves, with progress visible enough to keep both of them confident.
trifecta_alignment.mission: Freeing a competent team from work a system should do, so operations scale without burning people out.

cost_of_inaction: The team's week keeps a hidden tax: hours of copy-paste between systems, follow-ups that slip when someone's on leave, onboarding that takes weeks because the process lives in workarounds, and an ops lead whose own time goes to bridging tools instead of improving the operation. Growth makes every one of these worse, never better.
trigger_events: Headcount grew but throughput didn't, and the owner asked her why.
A dropped handoff (missed follow-up, double booking, lost enquiry) escalated to the owner or a key customer.
She mapped a process for a new hire and realized how much of it is manual bridging between tools.
An off-the-shelf tool they bet on hit its ceiling, and the workarounds now have workarounds.
The owner came back from a conference asking what they're doing about AI, and she needs a practical answer.
hiring_threshold: 1. FRICTION IS FELT DAILY: she can list the manual bridges and the hours they eat without opening a document. 2. TRUST IS ESTABLISHED: the partner explains things clearly enough for her to relay to the owner, shows real similar work, and gives her direct access to the person building. 3. THE FIRST STEP IS SMALL: one workflow automated end to end, visible to the whole team, before the broader engagement.
